source.title_on_document: Generative AI adoption in human creative tasks: Experimental evidence

supplement.where: Appendix E (p. 21): 'Supplementary material related to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414.'
supplement.holds: Preregistration and deviations (Supplementary Section 1, incl. 1.2-1.3 on the evaluation method); instructions, training materials, evaluator instructions, screenshots and example ideas/images (Section 3, 3.5); robustness Tables S1-S7 (standardized grades, by theme, individual/team-level and idea-evaluator-level data, dropping 10 evaluators, top-two-alpha evaluators); mediation Tables S9-S10; Figure S1 (treatment effects by DAT quartile).

paper_design_summary: In a preregistered lab experiment at Nankai University, 246 students in wave 1 (2023) were randomly assigned to work alone (HI, control), alone with ChatGPT 3.5 access (HAT), or in anonymous two-person teams (HHT) on two incentivized tasks (tasks 2 and 3) asking for an idea for a creative picture described in under 100 Chinese characters; task 1 was done alone by all. A second wave (2024) added 56 students in a Training arm (three ChatGPT training sessions, then the HAT procedure), compared with wave-1 arms without random assignment. Thirty student evaluators per task rated each idea for creativity on a 1-10 scale, text-only and with a DALL-E 3 image generated from the idea (image-text grade is primary); ten ChatGPT-generated ideas per theme were rated alongside.

studies.label: Wave 1 lab experiment (HI vs HAT vs HHT), picture-idea tasks 2-3

assignment.what_was_assigned: Treatment for tasks 2 and 3: work alone without AI (HI/Control), alone with ChatGPT 3.5 access (HAT), or in randomly matched anonymous two-person teams (HHT). Theme order in tasks 2-3 was randomized/counterbalanced.
assignment.quote: In the first wave, 246 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to one of three between-subject treatments.
assignment.locator: p. 2, Introduction; also p. 4, Section 2.1 and Table 1
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 6, Section 2.3: 'Our experimental design and intended analyses were pre-registered at AsPredicted.org.' Deviations in Supplementary Section 1 (not in this PDF).

arms.name: HI (Control)
arms.description: Tasks 2 and 3 done individually without ChatGPT (all participants had 12 minutes of free ChatGPT familiarization before task 1).

arms.name: HAT (human-AI team)
arms.description: Tasks 2 and 3 done individually with access to ChatGPT 3.5 via poe.com.

arms.name: HHT (human-human team)
arms.description: Tasks 2 and 3 done in anonymous two-person teams with random (re)matching for each task (61 teams), chatting by text and submitting one idea.

participants.exclusions: One HAT participant excluded from grade analyses because all ChatGPT interaction data were missing (chat-history export error) (p. 17, Appendix B.2). Image-text submissions are fewer than text-only ones (missing images: 46 of 784 prompts refused by DALL-E 3 content restrictions; some evaluator omissions), so image-text analyses cover fewer ideas, not fewer named people. Arm counts at assignment are given in Table D.2 and Appendix B.2 (63, 61, 122). n_analyzed 245 = 63 + 60 + 122 is derived from those counts and matches Table 2 text-only submissions (126, 120, 122).
participants.who: University students (undergraduate and graduate) at Nankai University; mean age about 21; majors mostly social sciences and STEM (Table D.2).
participants.quote: A total of 302 subjects completed our experiment, randomly distributed across four groups: 63 in the control group, 61 in the treatment group, 56 in the training group, and 122 in the team group.
participants.locator: p. 17, Appendix B.2; p. 19, Table D.2 (No. subjects 63, 61, 122; sessions 2, 2, 5)

ai_tool.how_used: HAT participants could freely prompt ChatGPT 3.5 while doing tasks 2 and 3 (on average 15 prompts over the two tasks; 59.27 percent of words in submitted ideas appear in ChatGPT responses). All arms had 12 minutes of free ChatGPT interaction before task 1 with brief prompting guidance (pp. 4, 6-7).

task.description: Generate an idea for a creative picture on a theme ('Surprisingly, he/she/it is here!' or '... is learning this new skill!') and describe it in fewer than 100 Chinese characters; experimenters turned each idea into an image with DALL-E 3. Incentivized: linear pay in average rating plus tournament bonus (p. 5).

outcomes.name: Image-text creativity grade (average rating of text plus DALL-E 3 image)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 30 student research assistants per task, blind to treatment, rated each idea 1-10 (one decimal) with the DALL-E 3 image shown; grade = average across evaluators. Cronbach's alpha 0.89 ('here') and 0.86 ('skill') (p. 6). Robustness variants: standardized grades (Table 2; Table S1), by theme (Tables S2-S3), individual/team-level and idea-evaluator-level data (Tables S4-S5), dropping 10 evaluators (S6), top-two-alpha evaluators (S7), all in the supplement. Heterogeneity by baseline DAT (Table 4, Fig. 2) shows an inverted U.

contrasts.reported: Table 2 Panel A non-standardized grades: Control 5.93 (2.30), HAT 6.18 (2.20); No. submissions 116, 116. Standardized: -0.14 (1.03) vs -0.00 (1.00). Table 3 random-effects, SE clustered by session: HAT 0.260*** (0.052) col 1 no controls, N = 442; 0.240*** (0.062) col 2; 0.229*** (0.060) col 3 full controls, N = 548. Text: 'improves creative performance by 0.24 points (0.32 SDs, p < .01) compared to the HI treatment, whose mean grade is 5.93 points.'
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2 Panel A and Table 3 cols 1-3; p. 2 and p. 7 text

contrasts.reported: Table 2 Panel A: HAT 6.18 (2.20), n = 116 submissions; HHT 6.28 (2.22), n = 106 submissions. Table 3 col 2: HHT 0.307*** (0.066) vs HAT 0.240*** (0.062) relative to Control. Text: 'The difference in the grades between the two wave-1 treatments is not statistically significant (p = .353).'

outcomes.name: Text-only creativity grade (average rating of the submitted text alone)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 30 student evaluators rated the text without the image (order of text-only and text-plus-image evaluation counterbalanced across evaluators). Cronbach's alpha 0.72 ('here') and 0.71 ('skill') (p. 6). Standardized variant in Table 2 Panel B.

contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2 Panel B and Table 3 cols 4-6

contrasts.reported: Table 2 Panel B: HAT 6.22 (2.16), n = 120; HHT 6.31 (2.15), n = 122. Table 3 col 5: HAT 0.090 (0.094), HHT 0.185** (0.091) relative to Control. No direct HAT-HHT test printed for text-only grades.

outcomes.name: Inequality of creative performance: coefficient of variation of grades and Gini coefficient of potential payments, by theme
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Dispersion of the image-text grades within each arm and theme: CV = SD / mean of the grade; Gini of payments under a linear rule with no fixed payment. Measures inequality of rated quality across people, not similarity of content. No test or interval printed.

contrasts.reported: Table 5: CV 'Here' Control 0.072, HAT 0.062; 'Skill' 0.155, 0.137. Gini 'Here' 0.040, 0.035; 'Skill' 0.089, 0.077. Text: access to ChatGPT 'reduces both the CV and the Gini coefficient'.

outcomes.name: Post-treatment Divergent Association Task (DAT) score and modified-DAT score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT: 10 nouns as different as possible, translated to English (Alibaba API), mean pairwise GloVe semantic distance x 100 (Appendix B.1). Modified DAT: six given words, one maximally dissimilar noun each, mean GloVe distance. Taken after task 3 in Questionnaire II, without ChatGPT; regression on post score controlling for pre score (eq. C.5). The paper reports effects in SDs from a coefficient plot only. Coded flexibility because DAT scores variety among one person's own words; reviewers may prefer overall_creativity.

contrasts.reported: 'experiencing ChatGPT access and experiencing teamwork both lead to an increase of 0.19 SDs in the modified-DAT score; their effect on the DAT score are not statistically significant.' Fig. 4b coefficient plot with 95% CIs.

studies.label: Wave 2 Training arm (ChatGPT after three training sessions), compared with wave-1 arms

assignment.quote: For these reasons, we do not interpret the difference between the Training treatment and the HAT treatment, if any, as a rigorously identified causal effect of training.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Introduction; p. 5, Section 2.1; Appendix A.3 pp. 16-17

arms.name: Training

arms.name: HI (Control), wave 1

participants.exclusions: 56 recruited; one Training participant excluded from grade analyses for not following DAT instructions (p. 17, Appendix B.2). Appendix B.2 describes all 302 as 'randomly distributed across four groups', which conflicts with the separate-wave description on pp. 3 and 5. n_analyzed 55 matches Table 2 text-only submissions (110).

data_and_code.data_url: Data will be made available on request (p. 15).

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned 246 students to no AI (HI, 63), ChatGPT 3.5 (HAT, 61) or human teams (HHT, 122); the HAT vs HI contrast alone has 123 people analyzed (63 + 60), well above 50. Outcome is creativity of each idea rated by 30 blind evaluators. The Training arm (S2) is not randomized relative to the wave-1 arms and is context only (quasi_people); S3 is ai_vs_human context.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT access raised the image-text creativity grade by 0.24 points (0.32 SDs, p < .01) over the no-AI control mean of 5.93 (Table 3 col 2: 0.240, SE 0.062; p. 7-8), less than human teams (0.31 points) and with a smaller, insignificant effect on text-only grades (0.090, SE 0.094).
open_questions: Table D.2 shows each treatment ran in its own sessions (HI 2, HAT 2, HHT 5, Training 2 sessions), and SEs are clustered by session with 11 clusters. The paper says participants were randomly assigned, but treatment appears to vary at the session level; the extraction should check the supplement on how assignment worked.

The '0.32 SDs' for the HAT effect (p. 7) uses the SD of the regression outcome (Appendix C, p. 18), but Table 2 prints a grade SD of 2.30 for the control arm. Which SD the paper uses is unclear; the extraction should not take '0.32 SDs' at face value as a control-SD standardized effect.

Appendix B.2 says all 302 subjects were 'randomly distributed across four groups', while pp. 3 and 5 say the Training arm was a separately recruited second wave and not causally comparable. S2 is coded quasi_people on the main-text description.

The primary outcome (image-text grade) was chosen after wave 1 (footnote 2; deviations in Supplementary Section 1, not on file); whether the preregistration named a primary outcome cannot be checked from this PDF.
Task type coded design_visual (text description of a picture, rated with a DALL-E 3 image); idea_generation is a defensible alternative.
Task 1 (all alone, pre-treatment) grades are not reported in the main text or appendix; task 4 (chosen via BDM) grades are not reported.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as outcomes (not scored on output): satisfaction, self-efficacy, meaningfulness, opinions about AI, self-rated skills (Fig. 4, pp. 11-12), and WTP for ChatGPT access (Table 6, Fig. 3). Process/mediation measures (word-overlap percentage, keyword origin UserFirst/AIFirst, Table 7) and the image-text vs text-only grade gap (Table 8, Fig. D.1) are mechanism analyses, not separate creativity outcomes. Heterogeneity by baseline DAT (Table 4, Fig. 2): inverted U, peak near DAT 80-83. n_units for S1-O1 (442) and S1-O2 (478) are the Table 3 col 1/col 4 observation counts, which include the Training arm (S2); HHT expanded to individual level gives 548 and 600. No diversity (across_people) outcome is reported.
